name: retrocore
description: 6502 and Z80 assembly and BASIC with source-level debugging on emulated Apple II family computers and the TRS-80 Model I.

scripts.compile: npm run generate:grammar && node scripts/copy-schema.mjs && tsc -p .
scripts.test:grammar: npm run check:grammar && node --test out/test/grammar.test.js out/test/basicGrammar.test.js out/test/pascalGrammar.test.js out/test/display.test.js out/test/pictures.test.js out/test/hardware.test.js out/test/machines.test.js out/test/startFlow.test.js out/test/favorite.test.js out/test/memory.test.js out/test/drives.test.js out/test/cycles.test.js out/test/project.test.js
scripts.test: npm run compile && npm run test:grammar && npm run test:editor

colors.description: The background of the lines a Retrocore assembly source's .if blocks leave out for the active target.
The overview ruler's mark for the lines a Retrocore assembly source's .if blocks leave out for the active target.

retrocore.languageServer.enabled.description: Run the retrocore language server: errors as you type, go to definition, hover, completion and symbols.

retrocore.languageServer.host.description: Path to Retrocore.Debug.dll. Empty uses the workspace build under artifacts/AnyCPU/Release/Retrocore.Debug/net11.0.

retrocore.inactiveCode.shade.description: Shade the lines of a Retrocore assembly source that the active target's .if blocks leave out, across the whole line and in the overview ruler, as the language server reports them. The server fades their text as well; the colors are retrocore.inactiveCodeBackground and retrocore.inactiveCodeOverviewRuler.

retrocore.lint.unlinkedNameWords.description: Prose terms the unlinked-name lint does not require links for. User and workspace lists are combined.

retrocore.basic.dialect.markdownDescription: The BASIC of a `.bas` file with no `REM retrocore` pragma and no dialect extension (such as `.applesoft.bas`). Empty uses the BASIC of the machine being debugged.

enumDescriptions: Keeps the machine's panel, dimmed, with Restart, Start Machine and Close.
Closes the machine's panel.
retrocore.display.onSessionEnd.markdownDescription: What the machine's display panel does when its debug session ends.

retrocore.favorites.markdownDescription: Machines kept under a name, listed in the Retrocore activity bar's **Favorites** view and first in **Start Machine** and **Switch Machine**. In user settings a favorite is in every workspace; in the workspace's settings it is shared with the project. Paths inside the workspace are written as `${workspaceFolder}/...`. Add one with **Add to Favorites** on the Machine view.

name.description: The favorite's name, which also names its launch configuration.

machine.description: The machine, as Start Machine lists it.

options.description: The machine's settings that differ from their defaults, by launch option, such as { "ramKilobytes": 32 }.

run.description: What it runs, when not just the machine.

dos.description: For a source on a fresh DOS disk, DOS 3.2 (13-sector) rather than 3.3.

machineState.description: Its cards and media, as the debugger saves them: { "cards": { "5": "diskII16" }, "media": { "slot5disk1": { "path": "...", "writeProtected": false } } }.

viewsWelcome.contents:
No machine is set up yet.
[Start Machine](command:retrocore.startMachine)
[Set Up a Machine](command:retrocore.machine.switch)
Set one up to add cards and insert disks before it starts, or pick a machine under Retrocore in the Run and Debug dropdown and press F5.
The machine's disk, tape and hard disk drives show here, with their media.

No favorites yet. The heart on the machine in the Machine view saves it here, with its settings, cards and disks: empty when it is not saved, filled when it is, broken when it has changed since.
[Save the current machine to favorites](command:retrocore.favorite.add)
Favorites are in your user settings, in every workspace; Share with Workspace puts one in the project's settings.

Start a retro machine without a launch.json: the Apple II family or the TRS-80 Model I.
[Start Retro Machine](command:retrocore.startMachine)

view/item/context.when: view == retrocore.favorites && viewItem =~ /\bfavorite\b/ && viewItem =~ /\buser\b/ && workbenchState != empty

project.description: A Retrocore project to build and debug: its retrocore.json, or the folder that holds it. The target supplies machine, model, rom, its options and its cards; project replaces source, program, debugFile, basic, executable and basicSource, and decides dialect, linkerConfiguration, loadAddress, entryAddress and dos.

target.description: With project: the target to build and debug, by name, or as project/target where a root retrocore.json's projects share one.

enumDescriptions: The Apple II family; model says which.
The Apple III.
The TRS-80 Model I.
The TRS-80 Model III, 4 or 4P; model says which (3 by default).
The TRS-80 Model 4: trs80-model3 with model 4 by default.
The TRS-80 Model II, 12 or 16 (its Z80 side); model says which (2 by default).
The TRS-80 Model 100 or Tandy 102: an 80C85, the 240x64 LCD and 8-32 KB, from your ROM; model says which (100 by default).
The Apple-1, with the Woz Monitor and the Apple Cassette Interface.
The TRS-80 Color Computer 1, 2 or 3; model says which.
The Commodore PET: the 2001 with BASIC 1 or the BASIC 2 upgrade ROMs, or the 4032 with BASIC 4; model says which (pet2001-basic2 by default).
The MITS Altair 8800: an 8080 with RAM and a terminal on the 88-2SIO; it has no ROM.
The Kaypro II: a 2.5 MHz Z80, 64 KB, 80x24 and two drives, running CP/M 2.2.
The BBC Micro, Model B or A; model says which (bbcb by default).
The Atari 800 or 400; model says which (atari800 by default).
The older name for apple2, from when only the IIe was emulated.
machine.description: The machine to emulate: apple2 is the Apple II family (model picks the IIe or enhanced IIe), apple3 an Apple III, trs80-model1 a TRS-80 Model I, trs80-model3 a Model III, 4 or 4P, trs80-model2 a Model II, 12 or 16, trs80-model100 a Model 100 or Tandy 102, apple1 an Apple-1, coco a TRS-80 Color Computer (model picks 1, 2 or 3), pet a Commodore PET (model picks the 2001 with BASIC 1 or 2, or the 4032), altair a MITS Altair 8800, kaypro2 a Kaypro II, bbc a BBC Micro (model picks the Model B or A), and atari800 an Atari 800 or 400 (model picks which).

romDirectory.description: Directory of externally supplied ROM dumps; defaults to RETROCORE_IIE_ROMS for the IIe, RETROCORE_IIPLUS_ROMS for the II Plus, RETROCORE_II_ROMS for the II, RETROCORE_APPLE3_ROMS for the Apple III (MAME's apple3 set), RETROCORE_TRS80_ROMS for the Model I, III, 4, 4P, II, 12 and 16 (the Model III, 4 and II families' dumps are under MAME's names, in the directory or its trs80m3, trs80m4, trs80m4p, trs80m2 or trs80m16 folder), RETROCORE_APPLE1_ROMS for the Apple-1 (wozmon.bin and aci.bin), RETROCORE_COCO_ROMS for the Color Computer, RETROCORE_PET_ROMS for the PET (MAME's pet2001, pet2001n, pet4016 and pet4032b chips, in the directory or its folder for the set) and RETROCORE_KAYPRO_ROMS for the Kaypro II (81-149c.u47 or 81-149c.rom, and 81-146.u43 or 81-146a.bin, in the directory or its kayproii folder), RETROCORE_BBC_ROMS for the BBC Micro and RETROCORE_ATARI_ROMS for the Atari 400 and 800. Without dumps the ROMs are assembled from the SDK's sources, which are byte-identical to them; the Color Computer's dumps are under MAME's names (such as bas12.rom, extbas11.rom, coco3.rom and disk11.rom), in the directory or its coco, coco2b, coco3 and coco_fdc folders, and the BBC Micro's too (os12.rom, basic2.rom, dnfs120.rom and saa5050), in the directory or its bbcb, bbc_acorn8271 and saa5050 folders, and the Atari's too (MAME's a800 and a800pal chips, such as co12399b.rom, co12499b.rom and co14599b.rom), with the 810's firmware in an atari810 folder beside them and Atari BASIC as basic-revc.rom (or -reva or -revb) in the directory or its basic folder. The Model 100 and Tandy 102 default to RETROCORE_TRS80M100_ROMS, and need m100rom.m12 or m102rom.m12 (or m100.bin, m100rom.bin, t102.bin, t102_rom.bin or m102rom.bin) there or in its trs80m100, tandy102 or trs80m100-roms folder.

highRam.description: Apple-1: a 4 KB bank of RAM at $E000-$EFFF, where BASIC loads and runs.

enumDescriptions: Altair 8800: MITS's disk boot loader at $FF00, which boots the 88-DCDD's drive 0.
Altair 8800: MITS's multi-boot loader at $FE00, which loads a MITS tape from the device the sense switches A11-A8 name.

proms.description: Altair 8800: the boot PROMs fitted, assembled from the SDK's sources or sdkRoms; DBL by default with the 88-DCDD, none without it.

cassetteInterface.description: Apple-1: the Apple Cassette Interface in the expansion slot, started from the Monitor with C100R. Altair 8800: the 88-ACR cassette interface at ports $06 and $07.

loadBasic.description: Apple-1: puts Apple-1 BASIC in the $E000 bank at power-on, as loading its tape would (basic.bin from romDirectory, or the SDK's build); E000R starts it. Needs highRam. A basic launch starts it itself.

rom.description: Model I and Model III: level2 or level1, Level II or Level I BASIC. Kaypro II: the monitor ROM dump's file name in romDirectory; by default 81-149c.u47 or 81-149c.rom. Model 100 and Tandy 102: the 32 KB ROM's file, a path or a name in romDirectory.

bootRom.description: Model II, 12 and 16: the boot ROM dump's file name in romDirectory; by default the newest of u54.u11, cpu_fc86.u11, cpu_2119.u11, cpu_11be.u11, 8047316.u11 and 8043216.u11 found.

optionRom.description: Model 100 and Tandy 102: an option ROM's file, up to 32 KB, which port $E0 bit 0 puts over $0000-$7FFF.

ramImage.description: Model 100 and Tandy 102: a file that keeps the RAM between sessions, as the battery does. When it exists it loads before the power comes on and the ROM carries on; when it does not, the machine starts cold. The RAM is saved to it as the session ends.

files.description: Model 100 and Tandy 102: host files to put in RAM's directory, so the menu lists them: .ba, .do and .co files as the Model 100 holds them, BASIC text as .bas (tokenized as Model 100 BASIC) and text as .txt. Each is named after its file, up to six letters and digits; one of a name already in RAM replaces it.

coldStart.description: Model 100 and Tandy 102: start from empty RAM even when ramImage exists, and replace it as the session ends.

time.description: Model 100 and Tandy 102: the clock's time to start at, as an ISO 8601 date and time; the host's by default. A cold start clears the date, as the ROM does.

revision.description: Model I: the Level II revision; 1.3 reads the dumps' _alt parts.

ramKilobytes.description: Model I: RAM in kilobytes, 4-48; defaults to 48 with the Expansion Interface, else 16 (4 for Level I). Apple II and II Plus: 16, 32 or 48 (the default) on the board. Apple III: 128, 256 (the default) or 512. Apple-1: 4 (the default), 8, 16 or 32 from $0000. Color Computer 1 and 2: 4, 16, 32 or 64 (16 on a CoCo 1, 64 on a CoCo 2); CoCo 3: 128 (the default) or 512. Model III: 16, 32 or 48 (the default). Model 4 and 4P: 64 or 128 (the default). Model II, 12 and 16: 32 to 512 in 32K banks, 64 by default. Altair 8800: 1 to 64 from $0000, 64 by default. PET: 4, 8, 16 or 32; 8 by default, or 32 on a 4032 (16 is the 4016). Atari 800 and 400: 8 to 48 in steps of 8; 48 on the 800 and 16 on the 400 by default. Model 100 and Tandy 102: 8, 16, 24 or 32 (the default), filled down from $FFFF.

switches.description: Altair 8800: the front panel's 16 address/data switches; the high 8 are the sense switches IN $FF reads.

baudRate.description: Altair 8800: the terminal's baud rate, on the 88-2SIO and the 88-SIO, which sets how fast characters reach the terminal and keys reach the program.

enumDescriptions: Altair 8800: the terminal is on the 88-2SIO's first port, at ports $10 and $11.
Altair 8800: the terminal is on the 88-SIO, at ports $00 and $01.
console.description: Altair 8800: the serial board the terminal is on. Altair BASIC picks its terminal by the sense switches: 4K BASIC 3.2 uses the 88-SIO with them down and the 88-2SIO with A11 up; the 4.0 BASICs use the 88-2SIO with them down and the 88-SIO with A13 up.

upperCase.description: Altair 8800: caps lock, so typed letters go out as capitals, as Altair BASIC needs.

expansionInterface.description: Model I: the Expansion Interface (RAM above 16K, the clock interrupt, disks); defaults on for Level II.

diskInterface.description: BBC Micro Model B: the Intel 8271 disk interface, with DNFS 1.20 in paged ROM socket 0. On by default; off, the Model B has tapes only and PAGE is &E00.

anyOf.description: Model I: the Expansion Interface's disk controller; defaults on when disks are given, since with a controller and no disk the ROM waits for one. Model III, 4 and 4P: the FD1793, likewise on when disks are given. Color Computer: the disk controller cartridge with Disk Extended Color BASIC; defaults on when disks are given. Altair 8800: the 88-DCDD floppy controller with four 8-inch drives; defaults on when disks are given.

enumDescriptions: IIe: the Disk II in slot 6, the default for WOZ and DOS-order images, and with diskBootRom.
IIe: the slot 7 block device, the default for .po images.

diskController.description: Model I: true or false, whether the Expansion Interface has its disk controller (on by default when disks are given). Color Computer: true or false, whether the disk controller cartridge is in the slot (on by default when disks are given). IIe: diskII or slot7, where diskImage goes (the Disk II in slot 6, or the slot 7 block device for .po images).

lowercase.description: Model I: the lowercase modification's seventh video bit. Color Computer 1 and 2: the MC6847T1 VDG, which shows lowercase, as on the CoCo 2B.

characterGenerator.description: Model I: the font: the stock MCM6670P, or Radio Shack's lowercase kit's replacement (as xtrs reconstructs it); defaults to kit with lowercase.

snow.description: Model I: show video snow when the CPU reads or writes video RAM while the beam draws (off by default). PET: the same, as on the 2001's board (on by default on the 2001, off on the others).

doubler.description: Model I: a double-density doubler: percom (selected by $FE/$FF commands, as NEWDOS/80 expects), tandy (the Radio Shack doubler, selected by $80/$A0 sector writes) or both.

cassette.description: Model I, Model III and 4, and Color Computer: a .cas tape to play (500 baud on a Model III or 4). Apple-1: a .wav tape, which plays from the start of the session. Altair 8800: a .tap tape of bytes for the 88-ACR, which plays at 300 baud from the start of the session. BBC Micro: a .uef tape, or any file with a .inf file beside it, which goes on a tape as the MOS saves files. Atari 800 and 400: a .cas tape for the 410, or an .xex, which goes on a boot tape. Model 100 and Tandy 102: a .wav tape, which plays when the ROM runs the motor (CLOAD). The PET's are cassette1 and cassette2.

cassette1.description: PET: a .tap, .wav or .prg tape in the built-in Datasette, cassette #1, with PLAY down. A .prg goes in as the tape SAVE writes.

cassette2.description: PET: a .tap, .wav or .prg tape in the second Datasette, cassette #2, with PLAY down.

boot.description: BBC Micro: hold SHIFT as the machine starts, as SHIFT-BREAK does, so the filing system boots the disk in drive 0 (its !BOOT) or, without a disk interface, the tape.

fastCassette.description: Model I, Color Computer, PET, BBC Micro and Atari 800 and 400: run as fast as possible while the cassette motor runs, so tapes load and save quickly. Apple-1 and Altair 8800: the same while a tape plays or records; Model 100: while the motor moves a tape that plays or records. The machine's own timing is unchanged.

disks.description: Model I, III, 4 and 4P: JV1, JV3, DMK or IMD images for drives 0-3, chosen by extension or, for .dsk, by contents. Model II, 12 and 16: IMD, DMK or JV3 images of 8-inch disks. Apple III: DOS- or ProDOS-order (.po) or WOZ images for .D1, the built-in drive, then .D2-.D4. Color Computer: JVC (.dsk) images for drives 0-3, which put the disk controller in the slot. PET: .d64, .d67 or .g64 images for the first disk unit's drive 0, its drive 1, then the next unit's; without diskUnits, as many units as they need, from device 8. Kaypro II: IMG, DSK, IMD or DMK images of single-sided double-density 5.25-inch disks for drive A, then B. BBC Micro: SSD or DSD images for drives 0 and 1; a DSD's second side is drive 2 or 3. Atari 800 and 400: ATR or XFD images for D1:-D4:; an .xex boots from a disk built for it. Altair 8800: SIMH .dsk images of 8-inch disks (77 tracks of 32 137-byte sectors) for the 88-DCDD's drives 0-3, which fit the controller and the DBL PROM and boot drive 0.

diskUnits.description: PET: the device numbers of the dual disk drives on the IEEE-488 bus, such as [8, 9], each the diskModel. Each needs its ROMs, MAME's c4040 or c2040 set, in driveRomDirectory or romDirectory. A 4032 has one as 8 when the ROMs are found; [] leaves it out.

enumDescriptions: The 4040, with DOS 2.0: D64 disks.
The 2040, with DOS 1.2: D67 disks, each initialized with the I command before it is read.
diskModel.description: PET: what the diskUnits are, a 4040 (DOS 2.0) or a 2040 (DOS 1.2).

driveRomDirectory.description: PET: a folder with the drives' ROMs under MAME's names: the 4040's c4040 set (901468-14 to -16, 901466-04 and 901467) or the 2040's c2040 set (901468-06 and -07, 901466-01 and 901467), or a folder holding c4040 and c2040 folders, or one beside them. Defaults to romDirectory, then RETROCORE_PET_ROMS.

bootSeconds.description: Model I, III, 4 and Color Computer: emulated seconds the ROM runs before a program loads, to set up its RAM; defaults to 1 on a Model I, III or 4 and 2 on a Color Computer or an Atari when loading a program. Model 100 and Tandy 102: 3 when loading a program, else 0. Model II and Kaypro II: 0 by default. Apple II project launches: 0.25 by default, so the Monitor is set up for a bare program.

command.description: Kaypro II: a command typed at CP/M's first prompt, such as DIR or B:STAT, once the machine's disks are in their drives; MBASIC by default with basic.

controllers.description: Apple II: read game controllers (Xbox, PlayStation and others) into the game port while the machine runs, even with VS Code in the background. The first controller's left stick or d-pad is the joystick (paddles 0 and 1) and its A, B and X buttons are buttons 0, 1 and 2; a second controller is paddles 2 and 3. False leaves the paddles unconnected.

programmersAid.description: Apple II: put Programmer's Aid #1 in the II's D0 socket ($D000-$D7FF), from the romDirectory's dump if it is there and otherwise built from the SDK's source. CALL -12288 starts its hi-res graphics. Other models have no D0 socket.

fastDisk.description: IIe and Apple III (and the Model II while its disk controller works, and the Kaypro II, which take it only from the launch): run as fast as possible while any disk drive's motor turns, then return to the chosen speed. The machine runs the same cycles either way; only how fast they pass in real time changes. The display panel's Fast disk changes it while debugging.

enumDescriptions: The machine's real speed.
Twice the machine's clock.
Four times the machine's clock.
Eight times the machine's clock.
As fast as the host can run it.
speed.description: How fast the machine runs, as a multiple of its clock; the display panel's Speed changes it while debugging.

enumDescriptions: No sound, and no cost.

The IIe's speaker, in mono. Costs about 2% of emulation speed. On a Color Computer, its sound through the TV: the DAC, cassette and single-bit sound. On a PET, the VIA's CB2, as a speaker on the user port plays it. On a BBC Micro, the SN76489, in stereo. On an Atari, POKEY through the TV, in mono. On a Model 100, its piezo buzzer.

The speaker and the Mockingboard's two sound chips, in stereo, and the Mockingboard in slot 4 unless mockingboard is false. Slows emulation by about a quarter, because the chips' output is worked out every cycle.
sound.description: IIe, Color Computer, PET, BBC Micro, Atari and Model 100: what the display panel plays while the machine runs. Sound plays in time only at the machine's real speed (speed 1); the panel's Sound button changes it while debugging.

mockingboard.description: IIe: whether the Mockingboard is in slot 4. Off unless sound is mockingboard; the Retro Devices view's Add Card puts it in while debugging.

softCard3.description: Apple III: puts Microsoft's SoftCard /// in this slot (1-4; its boot disk looks from slot 4 down), so its CP/M disk boots. The Z80 shows as its own thread, SoftCard /// Z80. The slot must be free, not one of proFiles' slots. None unless given; the Retro Devices view's Add Card puts it in while debugging.

softCard.description: Apple II: puts Microsoft's Z80 SoftCard in this slot (1-7; the manual uses 4), so a CP/M diskImage boots. The Z80 shows as its own thread. Not slot 3 on a IIe, nor the Mockingboard's slot 4. None unless given; the Retro Devices view's Add Card puts it in while debugging.

enumDescriptions: A color monitor or television (the default on the Apple II family, the Apple III, the Color Computer and the Atari).
Apple IIe: an RGB card and color monitor, without the composite signal's fringing: white runs stay white to their edges, colored areas are solid, and text is white.
A black and white monochrome monitor: on an Apple II, every dot sharp, as double hi-res desktops need.
A green-phosphor monochrome monitor.
An amber-phosphor monochrome monitor.
screen.description: The monitor the video is shown on: color on the Apple II family, the Apple III, the Color Computer and the Atari, or a white, green or amber monochrome one on any machine (green is the default on the Apple-1, the Model I and the Kaypro II, which have no color; the PET 2001 is white, and with BASIC 2 green). The display panel's Screen menu changes it, and its choice is kept for later launches on machines that have it.

mouse.description: Apple II: the slot of an AppleMouse II-compatible mouse card, which a click on the display drives until Escape. None by default; the Retro Devices view's Add Card puts it in while debugging.

disk35.description: Apple II: the slot of a 3.5 disk controller that answers as Apple's Apple II 3.5 Disk Controller Card: a SmartPort with two SuperDrives. Slot 5 is the usual one. None by default; the Retro Devices view's Add Card puts it in while debugging.

disk35Images.description: Apple II: the disks in the 3.5 controller's drives 1 and 2: 400K or 800K Apple disks or 720K or 1440K MFM disks, as .po, .2mg, .hdv, .img or .dsk images. Drive 1 boots. Needs disk35.

slot.description: The card's slot: 1 to 7 on the Apple II (not 3 on a IIe), 1 to 4 on the Apple III.

image.description: A ProDOS-order image (.po or .hdv) of up to 65535 blocks for the ProFile; changes stay in memory.

proFiles.description: Apple II and Apple III: ProFile interface cards, each with Apple's ProFile hard disk. The Apple II card boots ProDOS from it; on the Apple III, SOS reaches it through .PROFILE in SOS.DRIVER (the System Utilities disk's is set for slot 4). None by default; the Retro Devices view's Add Card puts one in while debugging.

logpointLimit.description: The most lines logpoints write to the Debug Console each second; the rest are counted and reported. 0 lifts the limit.

diskImage.description: Disk image for drive 1: a .po image goes to the slot 7 block device, and a WOZ, .dsk or .do image to the Disk II in slot 6.

dos.description: Boots the program from a fresh DOS disk built from the SDK's DOS sources (3.2 uses the 13-sector Disk II): the program as a binary file and a HELLO that BRUNs it, in a Disk II in slot 6. The program must start at its first address.

dosYear.description: With dos 3.3, which DOS 3.3 to boot: 1983 (the 680-0210-A System Master's) or 1980 (the 680-0051 masters').

basicSource.description: Apple II and PET: source listing for BASIC's ROM and debugger map: native Retrocore modules by default, or Microsoft's MACRO-10 source with the machine's changes as an overlay.

diskSectors.description: Without diskBootRom, the Disk II's ROMs are assembled from the SDK's sources: the 16-sector card's (341-0027 and 341-0028) or the 13-sector card's (341-0009 and 341-0010).

diskBootRom.description: Externally supplied 256-byte Disk II P5/P5A boot ROM, instead of the SDK's; selects native floppy I/O.

diskSequencerRom.description: Externally supplied 256-byte Disk II P6 sequencer PROM.

sequencerLayout.description: Explicit sequencer ROM pin/table layout: boot-socket for a dump read from the boot ROM's socket, as the known 341-0010 dump is.

enumDescriptions: The enhanced Apple IIe: a 65C02, MouseText and the enhanced firmware.
The original (unenhanced) Apple IIe: an NMOS 6502.
The Apple II Plus: AppleSoft and the Autostart Monitor, an NMOS 6502, 48 KB and a language card in slot 0.
The Apple II: Integer BASIC and the original Monitor (or, with monitor autostart, the Autostart Monitor), an NMOS 6502 and 48 KB.
The older name for iie-enhanced.
The older name for iie.
The Color Computer 1: Color BASIC with Extended Color BASIC, the MC6847 VDG and 16 KB.
The Color Computer 2: Color BASIC with Extended Color BASIC and 64 KB.
The Color Computer 3: Extended Color BASIC 2.0, the GIME and 128 KB.
The PET 2001 with the BASIC 2 upgrade ROMs, the 2001-N's: a green screen by default.
The 1977 PET 2001: BASIC 1, the white screen and the chiclet keyboard.
The PET 4032 (or, with 16 KB, the 4016): BASIC 4 with its disk commands, the graphics keyboard, and a 4040 as device 8 when its ROMs are found.
The PET 4032 with the business keyboard and its editor.
The BBC Micro Model B: MOS 1.20, BASIC II, 32 KB and, unless diskInterface is false, the 8271 with DNFS 1.20.
The BBC Micro Model A: MOS 1.20, BASIC II and 16 KB, with no disk interface.
The Atari 800: OS rev. B, Atari BASIC rev. C in the left slot, a right slot and 48 KB.
The Atari 400: the 800 with one cartridge slot and 16 KB.
TRS-80 Model III: a 2 MHz Z80, the Model III ROM, 48 KB and 64x16.
TRS-80 Model 4: 4 MHz, the Model III ROM, 128 KB, the memory maps and 80x24.
TRS-80 Model 4P: a Model 4 whose only ROM is a boot loader, with no cassette.
TRS-80 Model II: a 4 MHz Z80, 64 KB, 80x24 and 8-inch disks.
TRS-80 Model 12: the Model II's successor.
TRS-80 Model 16, 16B or Tandy 6000, its Z80 side only: the 68000 board is not emulated.
TRS-80 Model 100: the 1983 laptop's ROM, m100rom.m12.
Tandy 102: the Model 100 with its revised ROM, m102rom.m12.
model.description: Apple II: which model of the family. Color Computer: coco1, coco2 or coco3. PET: pet2001-basic2 (the default), pet2001, pet4032 or pet4032-business. BBC Micro: bbcb or bbca. Atari: atari800 or atari400. trs80-model3: 3, 4 or 4p. trs80-model2: 2, 12 or 16. trs80-model100: 100 or 102.

enumDescriptions: The revised chip: BASIC 1's 901447-09, or BASIC 4's 901465-23.
The original chip: BASIC 1's 901447-01, or BASIC 4's 901465-19.
basicRevision.description: PET 2001 and 4032: which of BASIC's revised chips is fitted, BASIC 1's first or BASIC 4's at $B000.

enumDescriptions: A language card: 16 KB of RAM at $D000-$FFFF, which DOS 3.3 loads the other BASIC into. The II Plus's default.
A firmware card with the other model's BASIC and Monitor in ROM: AppleSoft on a II, Integer BASIC on a II Plus. $C080 selects it and $C081 the board's ROM, as DOS 3.3's FP and INT do.
Nothing. The II's default.
slot0.description: Apple II and II Plus: the card in slot 0. The IIe's language card is built in.

enumDescriptions: The original Monitor: reset goes to the Monitor's * prompt; CONTROL-B starts Integer BASIC.
The Autostart Monitor of later IIs: power-on boots a disk or starts BASIC, and reset returns to BASIC.
Color Computer 3: a composite monitor or TV, the default.
Color Computer 3: the CM-8 RGB monitor, with the GIME's 64 colors as they are.
monitor.description: Apple II: its Monitor ROM. Color Computer 3: the monitor the GIME drives.

colorBasic.description: Color Computer 1 and 2: the Color BASIC ROM, bas10.rom to bas13.rom; 1.3 is the CoCo 2B's.

extendedBasic.description: Color Computer 1 and 2: the Extended Color BASIC ROM, extbas10.rom or extbas11.rom, or none; without dumps, built from the SDK's ExtendedBasic.asm.

diskBasic.description: Color Computer: the disk controller's Disk Extended Color BASIC ROM, disk10.rom or disk11.rom; without dumps, built from the SDK's DiskBasic.asm.

enumDescriptions: The colors most CoCo 1 and 2 machines show in 256-dot graphics, where RESET is pressed until they do.
The other phase.
Black and white dots, as on a monochrome monitor.
artifacts.description: Color Computer 1 and 2: the artifact colors a composite monitor shows in two-color graphics.

cartridge.description: Color Computer: a ROM pack image (.ccc or .rom, up to 16 KB) in the cartridge slot. Atari 800 and 400: a left cartridge (.rom or .car), in BASIC's place: basicCartridge is none by default with one.

rightCartridge.description: Atari 800: a cartridge for the right slot, which the 400 does not have: an 8 KB .rom, or a .car of the right-slot type.

enumDescriptions: Atari BASIC rev. C.
Atari BASIC rev. B.
Atari BASIC rev. A, as the first 400s and 800s had.
No BASIC: the left slot is empty, or holds the cartridge given.
basicCartridge.description: Atari 800 and 400: the revision of Atari BASIC in the left slot, from basic-revc.rom (or -revb or -reva) in romDirectory or its basic folder, or built from the SDK's source. none by default when cartridge is given.

enumDescriptions: NTSC: 60 Hz and a 1.79 MHz 6502.
PAL: 50 Hz and a 1.77 MHz 6502, with the PAL OS.
video.description: Atari 800 and 400: the video standard, which picks the OS: os on NTSC, the PAL OS on PAL.

enumDescriptions: OS rev. B.
OS rev. A, the first.
os.description: Atari 800 and 400 on NTSC: the OS ROM's revision. A PAL machine has the PAL OS.

enumDescriptions: The GTIA, with its three extra graphics modes (GRAPHICS 9-11).
The CTIA of the first machines, without them.
chip.description: Atari 800 and 400: the graphics chip ANTIC works with.

diskDrives.description: Atari 800 and 400: how many disk drives are on the serial bus, D1: to D4:. By default as many as disks names, or 1 for an executable.

enumDescriptions: The Atari 810, at the hardware level: its 6507 runs its firmware (rev. C), from an atari810 folder beside romDirectory's dumps or built from the SDK's source.
Drives that answer the serial bus's commands at the command level, without the 810's firmware.
diskDrive.description: Atari 800 and 400: how the disk drives are emulated.

executable.description: Atari 800 and 400: a binary load file (.xex), which boots from drive 1 on a disk built for it. disks then names no disk for drive 1.

autostart.description: Color Computer: whether the ROM pack starts itself through the CART interrupt, as games do.

enumDescriptions: Revision 1 and later: six hi-res colors.
Revision 0, the first boards: hi-res ignores bit 7, so four colors: black, white, green and violet.

firmwareCardRoms.description: Apple II and II Plus: the folder of the other model's ROM dumps the slot 0 firmware card holds; by default RETROCORE_IIPLUS_ROMS or RETROCORE_II_ROMS, or its folder (APPLE II+ or APPLE II) beside romDirectory, and without dumps the SDK's sources of them.

source.description: Native, ca65 or Merlin source to assemble with retrocore and load; replaces program and debugFile.

dialect.description: Dialect of source; defaults to native unless the file's first-line pragma names one.

hints.description: The hints file Retrocore Memory keeps marks, names and comments in, which --disassemble reads too. Defaults to <name>.hints.json beside the source, program or debug file, or for a project launch <project name>.<target>.hints.json beside its retrocore.json.

basic.description: A BASIC file to load and RUN: .applesoft.bas, .integer.bas, .apple1.bas, .level2.bas, .level1.bas, .colorbasic.bas, .petbasic.bas, .bbcbasic.bas, .atari.bas, or a .bas whose first line names its dialect. Numbered lines, or lines with labels; the machine boots to BASIC's prompt first. Replaces source and program.

run.description: With basic, or a PET program whose .prg loads at $0401: RUN the program once it is loaded; false leaves BASIC at its prompt.

program.description: Binary to load into RAM. PET: a .prg loads where its first two bytes say; one at $0401 is a BASIC program, which is RUN, and any other starts at its load address or entryAddress.

debugFile.description: cc65 .dbg (from ld65 or Retrocore.Debug --assemble) or VICE labels for program.

loadAddress.description: Load address of program, or origin of source when no linker configuration places it; defaults to $6000 on the IIe, $7000 on the Model I, $0800 on the PET and $E000 on the Model 100.

entryAddress.description: Starting PC; defaults to the load address, or the first section of source.

checkContracts.description: When a call to a routine with a ;; Keeps: section returns with a kept register, flag or memory location changed: report it in the Debug Console (warn), also stop there (stop), or do not check (off). With warn, ticking the Breakpoints view's Routine broke its Keeps: promise filter also stops.

checkUses.description: Also report registers a routine changed that its ;; Uses:, Out: and Keeps: sections do not list.

sdkRoms.description: Directory of the SDK's ROM sources to debug instead of the copy beside the debug host, so breakpoints set in those files bind: the Apple II's Roms directory (Slot7.rom.asm, AppleSoft, Microsoft6502Basic, System, IntegerBasic, DiskII, Dos), the TRS-80's (Level2.asm, Level1.asm, CharacterGenerator.asm, Model3.asm, Model4PBoot.asm, Model2Boot.asm and their character generators), the Color Computer's (ColorBasic.asm, ExtendedBasic.asm, DiskBasic.asm and Coco3.asm), the PET's (Basic/Basic1.asm, Basic2.asm and Basic4.asm, Basic1/Editor1.asm and Kernal1.asm, Basic2/Editor2.asm and Kernal2.asm, Basic4/Editor4.asm and Kernal4.asm, CharacterGenerator.asm and PetEquates.asm, with Microsoft6502Basic beside it as in the SDK), the Kaypro II's (Kaypro2.asm, Kaypro2CharacterGenerator.asm and MBASIC's modules in Mbasic), the Altair 8800's (Dbl.asm and Mbl.asm, which the PROMs are also built from), the BBC Micro's (Mos.asm, BbcBasic.asm, Dnfs.asm and Saa5050.asm, with their Mos, Basic and Dnfs folders), or the Atari's (its OS, floating point package, Atari BASIC and the 810's firmware).

breakpoints.description: Breakpoints to add before launching, once each: a file with a 1-based line, a label in a file whose first instruction to stop at, or a function breakpoint on a label or address expression.

label.description: A label in path; the breakpoint is on its first instruction.

function.description: A function breakpoint instead: a label or address expression, such as DISPLAY_CHAR or $C600.

condition.description: An expression that must be nonzero to stop, such as A == $0D.

hitCondition.description: Which hits stop: N or =N the Nth, >N, >=N, <N, <=N, or %N every Nth.

logMessage.description: Log this instead of stopping; {expression} shows a value, {expression,d} in decimal and {expression,c} as a character.
